full_judgment:
2. The appellant as pre-emptor filed Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 1991 before the Assistant Judge, Bancharampur against the pre-emptee respondent, Md. Mortuza Mollah and others under section 96 of the state Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (the Act, 1950) for pre-emption of the case land stating, inter alia, that the cm land belonged to Sonatan Saha and Khetra Mohan Saha in 4 annas share each and Darika Nath Saha in 8 annas share; ROR Khatian was prepared in the name of Sonatan Saha, Khetra Mohan Saha and the heirs of Darika Nath Saha. Sonatan Saha died leaving behind the pre-emptor as his only heir; Khetra Mohan Saha died leaving behind four sons named; Nemai Saha, Narayan Saha, Sobel Saha, Suboth Saha. Darika Nath died laving behind three sons named; Surendra, Narendra, Shachindra and they became the owners of his property and remained in possession therein in ejmali. Narendra transferred his share in favour of Sharaswati Rani Saha, the predecessor-in-interest of opposite party No. 6 (in the miscellaneous case) by registered deed of gift and delivered possession of the transferred land to her. Surendra said his share to the pre-emptor by an unregistered kabala and delivered possession of the transferred land to him. Shachindra out of his share sold 09 acre land to opposite party No. 3 (in the miscellaneous case) by a registered kabala dated the 29th day of December, 1976. The pre-emptor and opposite party Nos, 2 and 3 (in the miscellaneous case) are co-sharers in the case jote. Opposite party Nos.2 and 3 sold the case land to the pre-emptee by a registered kabala dated 02.01.1991 beyond the knowledge of the pre-emptor. The pre-emptor came to know about the kabala in question for the first time on 05.03.1991 from Sultan Moulavi, then he obtained the certified copy of the kabala on 07.03.1991 and came to know definitely that opposite 

 4. The trial Court by order dated 29.08.1993 rejected the pre-emption application on the findings, inter aria, that the case land being bhiti land was non-agricultural land, so the application filed under section 96 of the Act, 1950, was not maintainable; the application was barred by limitation; the kabala under pre-emption was a deed of exchange and not an out and out sale deed. However, the trial Court found that the pre-emptor was a co-sharer in the case holding and there was no defect of party in the case. 

 8. Mr. A.S.M. Khalequzzaman, learned Advocate, for the appellant, has reiterated the submissions on which leave was granted. He by referring to paragraph 9 of the pre-emption application has further submitted that in that paragraph, the pre-emptor categorically stated that he had in total three kanis land, he was an agriculturist and there was no legal bar in getting pre-emption of the case land. The assertions made in the said para-graph were not at all denied by the pre-emptee   in his written objection. He further submits that it was never the case of the pre-emptee that the pre-emptor owned land more than 60 bighas or that if the pre-emption of the case land was allowed, that would exceed the land ceiling as mandated in section 90 of the Act, 1950, but the High Court Division without considering the assertions made in paragraph 9 of the pre-emption application sent the matter back to the Appellate Court for haring the appeal afresh on the observation that "Appellate Court below was under obligation to frame a specific issue as to whether the total land of the petitioner will exceed the specific limit if, the pre-emption was allowed, as required under section 90 of the State Acquisition Tenancy Act, 1950 and failure to do so has caused an illegality occasioning failure of justice" and thus fell into an error in passing the impugned judgment and order and as such, the same is not sustainable in law and the appeal be allowed. 

 10. From the impugned judgment and order, it appears that the High Court Division, in fact, sent the case back to the Appellate Court to decide the only point whether the total land of the petitioner would exceed the ceiling of the land, i.e. 60 bighas land as mandated in section 90 of the Act, 1950, in case the pre-emption application was allowed. 

 12. This specific assertion of the pre-emptor as to the quantum of land owned by him was not denied by the pre-emptee in his written objection. Not only that, in the written objection of the pre-emptee, it was not stated that the pre-emptor owned land more than 60 bighas and if the pre-emption of the case land was allowed to him, it would exceed the ceiling as mandated in section 90 of the Act, 1950 and no point in that regard was ever raised by the pre-emptee either before the trial Court or before the Appellate Court. This was raised for the first time before the High Court Division during the hearing of the revision application. It needs to be mentioned further that even no ground was taken in the revision application. Whether the pre-emptor owned land more than 60 bighas as mandated in section 90 of the Act, 1950 was basically a question of fact and that could not be agitated for the first time before the High Court Division at the time of during hearing of the revision Moreso, the pre-emptor categorically stated in his application under section 96 of the Act, 1950 that he had only 3 (three) kanis land (three kanis is much less than 60 bighas) and that was not denied by the pre-emptee, but the High Court Division did not car to see the application filed under section 96 of the Act, 1950 and the written objection filed thereto. Therefore, the High Court Division was not at all justified in sending the appeal back to the Appellate court for deciding the question formulated by it as mentioned hereinbefore. 

 14. Be that as it may, we have considered the pleading of the parties and the evidence on record. Admittedly, the pre-emptor was a co-sharer in the case holding, whereas the pre-emptee was a stranger in the case holding. The kabala under pre-emption was registered under section 60 of the Registration Act on 14.01.1991 and the pre-emption application was filed on 07.05.1991, i.e. well within the period of 4 (four) months as provided in section 96 (1) of the Act, 1950. Therefore, the trial Court was absolutely wrong in holding that the pre-emption application was barred by limitation. The trial Court was also palpably wrong in holding that the pre-emption application was barred under the principle of estoppel, waiver and acquiescence on the view that the pre-emptor knew about the date of transfer in question prior to the date of knowledge of the transfer in question as stated in the application. Admittedly the pre-emption application was filed within the statutory period, mere knowledge of the transfer prior to the date of knowledge as mentioned in the application for pre-emption, in no way, can be construed as estoppel, waiver and acquiescence. In this regard, it needs to be mentioned that no case of estoppel, waiver and acquiescence was pleaded in the written objection. 

 15. The finding of the Appellate Court that the case land was an agriculture land, but not a non-agricultural land, so the application for pre-emption under section 96 of the Act, 1950 was maintainable in law, is based on proper appreciation of the evidence on record and the law governing the field. In this regard, it is necessary to keep on record that admittedly the case land is outside the municipal area, and merely because in the khatian, it was recorded as Bagan Bari, Bari and Bhiti and it did not become a non-agricultural land. Such kind of land clearly falls within the definition of agricultural land.
